chapter_text:
CHAPTER 16 — FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES

Introduction

A democracy is meaningful only if its citizens enjoy real freedom and protection from arbitrary state action. The Indian Constitution guarantees a set of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS in Part III (Articles 12-35). These are JUSTICIABLE — if violated, a citizen can directly approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for remedy. The Constitution also lays down DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (Part IV) that guide the government, and — added later by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 — FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Part IVA) that every citizen owes to the nation. This chapter studies all three.

16.1 FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS — SIX CATEGORIES

The Constitution originally provided SEVEN fundamental rights; the Right to Property was removed from this list by the 44th Amendment (1978), so today there are SIX:

(1) RIGHT TO EQUALITY (Articles 14-18)
 - Article 14: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws.
 - Article 15: prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
 - Article 16: equality of opportunity in public employment.
 - Article 17: ABOLITION OF UNTOUCHABILITY — its practice in any form is forbidden, an offence punishable by law.
 - Article 18: abolition of titles (no Maharaja, Knighthood, etc.; military and academic honours allowed).

(2) RIGHT TO FREEDOM (Articles 19-22)
 - Article 19: six freedoms — speech and expression; assembly peaceably and without arms; association or unions; free movement throughout India; reside and settle anywhere in India; practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business.
 - Article 20: protection in respect of conviction for offences (no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination).
 - Article 21: PROTECTION OF LIFE AND PERSONAL LIBERTY — 'No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' The Supreme Court has expanded this to include right to dignified life, privacy, environment, education, etc.
 - Article 21A: RIGHT TO EDUCATION — free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 (added by 86th Amendment, 2002).
 - Article 22: protection against arbitrary arrest and detention.

(3) RIGHT AGAINST EXPLOITATION (Articles 23-24)
 - Article 23: prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar).
 - Article 24: PROHIBITION OF CHILD LABOUR — no child below 14 can be employed in any factory, mine or hazardous employment.

(4) RIGHT TO FREEDOM OF RELIGION (Articles 25-28)
 - Article 25: freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion.
 - Article 26: freedom to manage religious affairs (including running institutions, owning property).
 - Article 27: no person can be compelled to pay any tax for the promotion of a particular religion.
 - Article 28: no religious instruction in state-funded educational institutions.

(5) CULTURAL AND EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS (Articles 29-30)
 - Article 29: protection of language, script and culture of minorities; no citizen can be denied admission to a state-aided educational institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.
 - Article 30: right of religious and linguistic minorities to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

(6) RIGHT TO CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (Article 32)
 - The 'right to enforce the other rights' — a citizen can directly approach the SUPREME COURT for the enforcement of any Fundamental Right. The Court can issue WRITS:
   * HABEAS CORPUS — 'produce the body' — used to free a person illegally detained.
   * MANDAMUS — 'we command' — directs a public authority to perform its duty.
   * PROHIBITION — stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction.
   * CERTIORARI — calls up the record of a lower court for review.
   * QUO WARRANTO — 'by what authority?' — questions a person's right to hold a public office.
 - Dr Ambedkar called Article 32 'the HEART AND SOUL of the Constitution'.
 - High Courts have similar power under Article 226.

16.2 NATURE AND LIMITATIONS OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS

Fundamental Rights are not ABSOLUTE — they come with REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS. For example, the right to free speech (Article 19) can be restricted in the interests of:
 - Sovereignty and integrity of India
 - Security of the state
 - Friendly relations with foreign states
 - Public order, decency, morality
 - Contempt of court, defamation
 - Incitement to an offence

During a NATIONAL EMERGENCY (Article 352), most Fundamental Rights — except those under Articles 20 and 21 — may be suspended.

Fundamental Rights apply MAINLY AGAINST THE STATE — that is, against arbitrary action by the government, its agencies and its officials. Some rights (Articles 17, 23 etc.) apply also between private parties.

16.3 DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY

Directive Principles (Articles 36-51) are GUIDELINES to the government when making policy. They are NOT JUSTICIABLE — courts cannot enforce them — but they are 'FUNDAMENTAL in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws' (Article 37).

Directive Principles can be grouped into:
 - SOCIALIST principles (welfare, reduction of inequality, right to work and education, equal pay).
 - GANDHIAN principles (village panchayats, cottage industries, prohibition of cow slaughter, prohibition of intoxicating drinks).
 - LIBERAL-INTELLECTUAL principles (uniform civil code, separation of judiciary from executive, free legal aid, environment protection, international peace).

16.4 FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Article 51A)

Added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the SWARAN SINGH COMMITTEE. Originally TEN duties; an eleventh was added by the 86th Amendment (2002) about parents' duty to provide education to children aged 6-14.

It shall be the duty of every citizen of India:
(a) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem;
(b) To cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom;
(c) To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India;
(d) To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so;
(e) To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women;
(f) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture;
(g) To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures;
(h) To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform;
(i) To safeguard public property and to abjure violence;
(j) To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement;
(k) [Added 2002] Who is a parent or guardian, to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.

Fundamental Duties are NOT JUSTICIABLE in themselves but the courts can take them into account when interpreting laws.

SUMMARY

- Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable rights guaranteed to every citizen — six rights: equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural-and-educational, constitutional remedies.
- Article 14 = equality before the law; Article 17 = abolition of untouchability; Article 21 = right to life and personal liberty; Article 32 = constitutional remedies.
- Fundamental Rights are not absolute; reasonable restrictions apply; most may be suspended during national emergency.
- Directive Principles (Part IV) are non-justiciable guidelines for government policy.
- Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, added 1976) are eleven duties of every citizen.

chapter_summary.title: Fundamental Rights and Duties — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 16 covers Part III, IV and IVA of the Indian Constitution — Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, and Fundamental Duties. Fundamental Rights are justiciable; Directive Principles are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance; Fundamental Duties are moral and civic obligations of every citizen.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Fundamental Rights and Duties
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Cite specific Article numbers wherever possible.

questions.question: List the six Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer: (1) RIGHT TO EQUALITY (Articles 14-18). (2) RIGHT TO FREEDOM (Articles 19-22). (3) RIGHT AGAINST EXPLOITATION (Articles 23-24). (4) RIGHT TO FREEDOM OF RELIGION (Articles 25-28). (5) CULTURAL AND EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS (Articles 29-30). (6) RIGHT TO CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (Article 32). [The Right to Property was originally a Fundamental Right but was removed from this list by the 44th Amendment in 1978; it is now an ordinary legal right under Article 300A.]

questions.question: What does Article 14 of the Constitution guarantee?
questions.answer: Article 14 reads: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' This contains two ideas: (1) EQUALITY BEFORE LAW — borrowed from British tradition — means absence of any special privilege; all persons are equal before the law of the land. (2) EQUAL PROTECTION OF THE LAWS — borrowed from the US Constitution — means that persons in similar circumstances should be treated alike; reasonable classification for legitimate purpose is permitted but arbitrary discrimination is not. Article 14 applies to all PERSONS (including non-citizens), not just to citizens.

questions.question: State the provisions of Article 17 (Abolition of Untouchability).
questions.answer: Article 17 states: 'Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of Untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.' This is a unique provision of the Indian Constitution. Parliament has enacted the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (originally the Untouchability Offences Act 1955) and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 to enforce Article 17. Untouchability is forbidden whether the discrimination is by the state, private institutions, or individuals. It is among the most significant social reforms accomplished by the Indian Constitution.

questions.question: List the six freedoms guaranteed by Article 19.
Why is Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) called the 'most important' Fundamental Right?
questions.answer:
Article 21 reads: 'No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' It applies to ALL persons (citizens and non-citizens). It is the most important right because:
(1) Without life and liberty, no other right is meaningful.
(2) The SUPREME COURT has interpreted 'life' VERY BROADLY — not mere animal existence but a life of DIGNITY. It has read into Article 21 a host of rights — right to a clean ENVIRONMENT (M.C. Mehta cases), right to PRIVACY (Puttaswamy, 2017), right to LIVELIHOOD (Olga Tellis), right to EDUCATION (Unni Krishnan), right to LEGAL AID, right to SHELTER, right to HEALTH, right to PERSONAL AUTONOMY etc.
(3) Unlike most Fundamental Rights, Article 21 CANNOT BE SUSPENDED even during a national emergency (a protection added by the 44th Amendment after the lessons of the 1975-77 Emergency).

questions.question: What does the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) provide?
questions.answer:
Article 23 prohibits:
 - TRAFFIC IN HUMAN BEINGS — selling and buying human beings, including for sexual exploitation.
 - BEGAR (forced labour without payment).
 - All other forms of FORCED LABOUR.
Violation is punishable. (The state can impose compulsory service for public purposes — e.g. emergency drafts — without discrimination.)

Article 24 prohibits CHILD LABOUR: 'No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.' Parliament has enacted the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 (now amended) to enforce this.

Together, Articles 23-24 protect the most vulnerable — the poor, women, children — from being exploited.

questions.question: What does the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28) include?
questions.answer:
Article 25 — Every person has FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE and the right to freely profess, practise and propagate any religion. Subject to public order, morality and health.
Article 26 — Every religious denomination has the right to MANAGE its religious affairs — establish institutions, own property, administer such property by law.
Article 27 — No person shall be COMPELLED TO PAY ANY TAX for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion.
Article 28 — NO RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of state funds. Educational institutions partially state-funded or state-recognised may give religious instruction only with the consent of the student (or guardian).

Together these articles establish India as a SECULAR STATE where religious freedom is guaranteed and the state stays equidistant from all religions.

questions.question: What is the significance of Article 32? Name the five writs.
questions.answer:
Article 32 — RIGHT TO CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES — allows any citizen to MOVE THE SUPREME COURT DIRECTLY for the enforcement of any Fundamental Right. The Court can issue WRITS (formal orders). Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR called it 'the very SOUL of the Constitution and the very HEART of it'. Without Article 32 the other Fundamental Rights would be empty words.

FIVE WRITS:
(1) HABEAS CORPUS — 'you shall have the body' — orders production of a detained person before the court; used to test the legality of detention.
(2) MANDAMUS — 'we command' — orders a public authority to perform a duty it has failed to perform.
(3) PROHIBITION — orders a lower court or tribunal to stop proceedings in which it has exceeded its jurisdiction.
(4) CERTIORARI — calls up records of a lower court to review a decision.
(5) QUO WARRANTO — 'by what authority' — questions a person's right to hold a public office.

questions.question: What are 'Directive Principles of State Policy'? How are they different from Fundamental Rights?
questions.answer:
DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES (Articles 36-51) are guidelines to the state on how to make policy. Examples: organising village panchayats, providing free legal aid, securing a uniform civil code, separating judiciary from executive, protecting environment, promoting cottage industries, etc.

DIFFERENCES FROM FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS:
  Fundamental Rights are JUSTICIABLE — citizens can sue the state if they are violated.
  Directive Principles are NON-JUSTICIABLE — no one can sue for their enforcement.
  Fundamental Rights are NEGATIVE — they tell the state what it CANNOT do.
  Directive Principles are POSITIVE — they tell the state what it SHOULD do.
  Fundamental Rights are aimed at ensuring INDIVIDUAL FREEDOM and equality.
  Directive Principles aim at SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC JUSTICE.

Though non-justiciable, Article 37 declares Directive Principles 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and the state's duty to apply them. Many have been implemented through legislation (e.g. minimum wages, panchayati raj, free legal aid).

questions.question: List the eleven Fundamental Duties of an Indian citizen (Article 51A).
questions.answer:
It shall be the duty of every citizen of India:
(a) To ABIDE BY THE CONSTITUTION and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
(b) To CHERISH AND FOLLOW the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom.
(c) To UPHOLD AND PROTECT the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
(d) To DEFEND THE COUNTRY and render national service when called upon.
(e) To PROMOTE HARMONY and the spirit of common brotherhood among all the people of India, transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the DIGNITY OF WOMEN.
(f) To VALUE AND PRESERVE the rich heritage of our composite culture.
(g) To PROTECT AND IMPROVE THE NATURAL ENVIRONMENT — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife — and to have compassion for living creatures.
(h) To develop the SCIENTIFIC TEMPER, humanism and spirit of inquiry and reform.
(i) To SAFEGUARD PUBLIC PROPERTY and abjure violence.
(j) To STRIVE TOWARDS EXCELLENCE in all spheres of individual and collective activity, so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement.
(k) [Added by 86th Amendment, 2002] Who is a parent or guardian, to PROVIDE OPPORTUNITIES FOR EDUCATION to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years.

These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

questions.question: What protections does Article 20 give to a person accused of an offence?
questions.answer: Article 20 gives three protections: (1) NO EX POST FACTO LAW — a person cannot be convicted under a law that was not in force at the time the act was done, nor punished with a greater penalty than the law provided then. (2) NO DOUBLE JEOPARDY — a person cannot be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. (3) NO SELF-INCRIMINATION — a person accused of an offence cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself.

questions.question: Why has the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 so broadly?
questions.answer: Because the Supreme Court has held that 'LIFE' in Article 21 does NOT mean mere ANIMAL EXISTENCE but a LIFE OF DIGNITY worth living. Through a long line of judgments — Maneka Gandhi (1978), Olga Tellis (1985), M.C. Mehta (environment cases), Unni Krishnan (right to education), K.S. Puttaswamy (2017, right to privacy) — the Court has read into Article 21 a host of unenumerated rights: right to PRIVACY, right to LIVELIHOOD, right to clean ENVIRONMENT, right to EDUCATION, right to LEGAL AID, right to SHELTER, right to HEALTH, right to PERSONAL AUTONOMY, right to die with dignity. This expansive interpretation has made Article 21 the workhorse of Indian constitutional law — the Court can address new threats to dignity (like data privacy) without amending the Constitution.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Article 25 (freedom of religion) and reform of unjust religious practices?
questions.answer: Article 25 guarantees freedom to profess, practise and propagate religion — BUT it is subject to PUBLIC ORDER, MORALITY and HEALTH, and to the other provisions of Part III. Article 25(2) explicitly allows the state to: (a) regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice; (b) provide for SOCIAL WELFARE AND REFORM, including the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. So the state can intervene to ABOLISH untouchability, OPEN TEMPLES to Dalits, BAN child marriage and dowry, REGULATE temple administration — even though some religious leaders may oppose such interventions. The Constitution thus respects religion but does not allow religion to override constitutional values of equality and human dignity.

questions.question: Explain the five writs the Supreme Court can issue under Article 32.
questions.answer:
(1) HABEAS CORPUS ('you shall have the body') — orders production of a person illegally detained; if detention is unlawful, the person is released. Used against arbitrary arrest.
(2) MANDAMUS ('we command') — orders a public authority (officer, board, court) to PERFORM a duty it has failed to perform.
(3) PROHIBITION — orders a lower court or tribunal to STOP proceedings that exceed its jurisdiction.
(4) CERTIORARI — calls up records of a lower court to QUASH a decision passed without jurisdiction or against the law.
(5) QUO WARRANTO ('by what authority?') — challenges a person's right to hold a public office and asks them to prove their legal title.
High Courts have similar power under Article 226, but with a wider scope (they can issue writs for any purpose, not only Fundamental Rights).

questions.question: Give three examples of Directive Principles and how they have been implemented.
questions.answer:
(1) Article 40 — ORGANISATION OF VILLAGE PANCHAYATS: implemented by the 73rd Amendment (1992), which made panchayati raj a constitutional institution with regular elections and reserved seats.
(2) Article 41 — RIGHT TO WORK, EDUCATION AND PUBLIC ASSISTANCE: partly implemented through schemes like MGNREGA (right to 100 days' rural work, 2005), and the Right to Education Act 2009 (Article 21A).
(3) Article 47 — PROHIBITION OF INTOXICATING DRINKS: implemented partially — some states like Gujarat, Bihar (re-imposed 2016), Mizoram have full prohibition.
(4) Article 48A — PROTECTION AND IMPROVEMENT OF ENVIRONMENT: implemented through Environment Protection Act 1986, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, etc.
(5) Article 39A — FREE LEGAL AID: implemented through the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987.
(6) Article 50 — SEPARATION OF JUDICIARY FROM EXECUTIVE: implemented through the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973.

So though Directive Principles cannot be directly enforced in court, many have driven major legislation.

questions.question: List five Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens.
questions.answer:
(Article 51A. Any five of the eleven duties.)
(a) To ABIDE BY THE CONSTITUTION and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and National Anthem.
(b) To CHERISH AND FOLLOW the noble ideals of our freedom struggle.
(c) To UPHOLD AND PROTECT the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
(d) To DEFEND THE COUNTRY and render national service.
(e) To PROMOTE HARMONY and the spirit of common brotherhood across diversity; renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
(g) To PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife.
(i) To SAFEGUARD PUBLIC PROPERTY and abjure violence.
(j) To STRIVE TOWARDS EXCELLENCE in all spheres.
(k) To PROVIDE EDUCATION to one's child aged 6-14 [added 2002].

questions.question: Why are Fundamental Rights not absolute? Give examples of reasonable restrictions.
questions.answer:
Fundamental Rights are not absolute because INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS must be balanced against COLLECTIVE INTERESTS — public order, security, decency. If absolute, freedom of speech could be used to incite riots; freedom of movement could be used to spread disease in a pandemic. The Constitution itself permits 'REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS'.

EXAMPLES:
 - FREEDOM OF SPEECH (Article 19) can be restricted in the interests of (a) sovereignty and integrity of India, (b) state security, (c) friendly relations with foreign states, (d) public order, (e) decency or morality, (f) contempt of court, (g) defamation, (h) incitement to an offence. Hence laws against hate speech, sedition, obscenity etc.
 - RIGHT TO ASSEMBLY can be restricted by imposing curfew or denying permission for a march in a sensitive area.
 - RIGHT TO PROFESSION can be restricted by requiring qualifying exams (e.g. medical licence) and barring some professions (e.g. selling liquor) where state policy dictates.
 - During a NATIONAL EMERGENCY (Article 352), most Fundamental Rights can be suspended — except Articles 20 and 21.
Reasonable restrictions must be (a) related to the listed grounds, (b) proportionate, (c) not arbitrary, (d) reviewable by courts.

questions.question: Why did Dr Ambedkar call Article 32 'the heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.answer:
Because Article 32 is the RIGHT TO ENFORCE all the other Fundamental Rights. Without an effective remedy, the most carefully drafted rights would be hollow declarations. Article 32 ensures that any citizen — rich or poor, educated or illiterate — can DIRECTLY approach the SUPREME COURT (without first going through lower courts) for the enforcement of a Fundamental Right. The Supreme Court can then issue any of the five WRITS (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto) to remedy the violation.

Ambedkar said in the Constituent Assembly: 'If I was asked to name any particular article in this Constitution as the most important — an article without which this Constitution would be a nullity — I could not refer to any other article except this one. It is the very SOUL of the Constitution and the very HEART of it.' Article 32 is therefore not just one Fundamental Right among others — it is the right that makes all the others REAL.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
questions.answer:
Both are essential parts of the Constitution but operate differently:
 - FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS are JUSTICIABLE — enforceable in court. They impose NEGATIVE OBLIGATIONS on the state (don't violate equality, don't restrict speech unreasonably).
 - DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES are NON-JUSTICIABLE — not enforceable in court directly. They impose POSITIVE OBLIGATIONS on the state (provide work, education, welfare).

In early years (Champakam Dorairajan, 1951), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights PREVAIL over Directive Principles in case of conflict. Over time, the Court evolved a more harmonious view — both should be read together; both are essential for justice; the state should try to implement Directive Principles WITHOUT violating Fundamental Rights. In some cases (e.g. expanding Article 21 to include education, livelihood, environment), Directive Principles have helped EXPAND the scope of Fundamental Rights. The two thus COMPLEMENT each other: rights protect against state arbitrariness; principles tell the state what to actively achieve.

questions.question: Describe in detail the six freedoms granted by Article 19.
questions.answer:
Article 19(1) of the Constitution guarantees to ALL CITIZENS six fundamental freedoms. Each is subject to 'reasonable restrictions' as specified in Article 19(2)-(6):

(a) FREEDOM OF SPEECH AND EXPRESSION — to express one's views by spoken word, writing, printing, art, gesture or any other medium. Includes freedom of the press, right to information, right to silence. Subject to restrictions on grounds of sovereignty, security, public order, decency, defamation, contempt of court, incitement to offence.

(b) FREEDOM TO ASSEMBLE PEACEABLY AND WITHOUT ARMS — meet for any peaceful purpose (rallies, protests, public meetings). Subject to restrictions on grounds of sovereignty and public order. Authorities may impose conditions (route, time), and may invoke Section 144 CrPC to ban assemblies.

(c) FREEDOM TO FORM ASSOCIATIONS, UNIONS OR CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES — including political parties, trade unions, cultural and religious associations. Subject to restrictions on grounds of sovereignty, integrity, public order, morality.

(d) FREEDOM TO MOVE FREELY THROUGHOUT INDIA — internal migration is allowed; no internal passports. Subject to restrictions in the interests of general public or scheduled tribes' protection (e.g. permits required for some tribal areas).

(e) FREEDOM TO RESIDE AND SETTLE IN ANY PART OF INDIA — corollary of (d). Subject to similar restrictions, and in special cases like J&K (under Article 35A till 2019).

(g) FREEDOM TO PRACTISE ANY PROFESSION, or carry on any occupation, trade or business — subject to professional qualifications, state monopolies (e.g. nuclear, defence), and reasonable regulation.

[Sub-clause (f) — RIGHT TO PROPERTY — was removed by the 44th Amendment 1978. Property is now an ordinary legal right under Article 300A.]

These six freedoms are at the core of personal liberty in India.
